title: New Pass-ta-key attack reveals all the things we didn't know about passkeys
gist: Palo Alto Networks researcher Arie Olshtein's 'Pass-ta-key' attack extracts all passkeys from Google Password Manager on malware-infected Windows machines, which Dan Goodin argues is neither novel nor a passkey flaw. The real disclosure is architectural: FIDO2 never mandated TPM storage, nearly all platforms keep passkeys locally or in E2E-encrypted cloud blobs, and Windows' one-directional sandboxing is the structural weak point that forced Google, 1Password and Dashlane to move Windows passkeys to servers.

themes.theme: FIDO2 never required hardware key storage

insights.claim: The FIDO 2 specifications managed by the FIDO Alliance do not mandate that passkeys be stored in TPMs, secure enclaves, trusted execution environments, or StrongBoxes, contradicting the widespread belief that passkeys live exclusively in hardened silicon.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Security-buyer assumptions about passkey hardware isolation are wrong, which matters for enterprise vendor selection and for how much credit hardware-security vendors deserve in the passkey rollout.
insights.quote: contrary to common belief, the FIDO 2 specifications—managed by the industry group FIDO Alliance—don’t mandate that passkeys be kept in TPMs, or any other sort of dedicated piece of hardware
insights.locator: The answer is that, contrary to common belief

insights.claim: Microsoft is virtually the only platform vendor offering TPM-backed passkey storage on Windows, and it recommends that option mainly to enterprises rather than consumers.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Hardware-rooted passkey storage is an enterprise-only niche, capping the addressable market for TPM-dependent authentication features.
insights.quote: Virtually the lone holdout is Microsoft, which gives users the option to store passkeys in the Windows TPM.
insights.locator: The answer is that, contrary to common belief

insights.claim: Passkey architects abandoned mandatory TPM storage because it made cross-device syncing impossible — the only way to load a passkey into a new device's TPM would be to re-create each one individually — and syncing was judged essential to adoption.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Usability beat hardware purity in authentication design; expect the same tradeoff to repeat in any credential system that needs mass consumer adoption.
insights.quote: The shift to local storage came a few years ago after OS and third-party application developers realized that passkeys had no chance of gaining widespread usage unless they could easily be synced to all of a user’s devices.
insights.locator: Unbeknownst to me until I began research for this article

insights.claim: Local on-device passkey storage has held up in practice on macOS, iOS and Android because granular app permissions prevent malware from reaching another app's private keys absent an exotic OS-level zero-day.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The mobile passkey model is empirically sound, so authentication risk concentrates on the desktop, not the phone — relevant to where security spend should go.
insights.quote: So far, these assumptions have been proven correct in real-world practice.
insights.locator: Ultimately, architects of the FIDO specifications decided

themes.theme: Windows sandboxing as the structural weak point

insights.claim: Windows apps generally run with all the privileges of the user, and Windows sandboxing protects in only one direction — an unsandboxed app such as malware can read a sandboxed app's data, which other platforms prevent by default.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Windows' backward-compatibility debt is a permanent, structural security discount versus Apple and Android platforms — a durable driver of third-party endpoint security demand on Windows specifically.
insights.quote: That is, the sandbox only protects in one direction.

insights.claim: The weaker Windows isolation model persists largely because of backward-compatibility requirements, meaning the vulnerability is a deliberate design constraint rather than a fixable bug.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Do not expect Microsoft to close this gap; the mitigation market (EDR, credential-guard products) stays structurally supported.
insights.quote: which is largely necessary for Windows backward-compatibility reasons
insights.locator: That means Windows malware has decidedly fewer problems

insights.claim: Because passkeys stored on Windows devices cannot be trusted to survive a malware infection, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Dashlane and other third-party apps on Windows store passkeys as end-to-end encrypted blobs on servers rather than locally.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Windows credential security is now a cloud-service dependency for all major password managers, concentrating systemic risk in a handful of vendor backends.
insights.quote: Server-stored passkeys are now the design used not just by GPM for Windows, but 1Password, Dashlane, and other third-party apps for the Microsoft OS as well.
insights.locator: That means Windows malware has decidedly fewer problems

insights.claim: In the Windows Google Password Manager flow, the device retrieves a user or device key from the TPM and presents it to Google's backend authenticator, and the Google server — holding the private key in encrypted form — issues the signed authentication assertion, so the login-critical signing happens server-side, not on the device.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Server-side assertion signing makes the identity provider a single point of compromise and a regulatory chokepoint for Windows authentication.
insights.locator: At a simplified level, here’s how it works

insights.claim: Pass-ta-key's most powerful variant makes an infected Windows machine masquerade as an iPhone, triggering Google Password Manager's device-migration sync so the full passkey set is transferred to the attacker-controlled machine.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Device-migration and sync flows are the highest-value abuse surface in credential systems — the place to look for the next disclosure and for product hardening.
insights.quote: The most powerful of the three attack variants causes the infected Windows machine to masquerade as an iPhone.
insights.locator: When your device is infected, all bets are off

insights.claim: The attack requires an already-malware-infected Windows machine that is signed in to the user's Google account, so it is a post-compromise credential-harvesting technique rather than an initial-access vulnerability in passkeys.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Framing matters for procurement: the fix is endpoint protection, not abandoning passkeys.
insights.locator: The malware in the Pass-ta-key attacks uses its access

insights.claim: Google Password Manager may lack protections present in competing password managers such as 1Password, which calls OS APIs to stop other processes from reading its memory.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A concrete feature-level differentiator for paid password managers versus the free bundled default — a wedge for 1Password-class vendors in enterprise deals.
insights.quote: it’s possible that GPM lacks some protections found in password managers like 1Password, such as calling OS APIs to restrict other processes from reading its memory
insights.locator: This risk has always been present

insights.claim: The stated purpose of passkeys is to eliminate a shared secret that can be phished or stolen in a server breach; they were never designed to withstand attacks against a compromised device that stores them.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Judge authentication products against their actual threat model — phishing and breach resistance — or you will misprice both the technology and the vendors selling around it.
insights.quote: The purpose of passkeys is to eliminate a shared secret that can be phished or obtained through server breaches. Passkeys aren’t intended to withstand physical attacks against the devices that store them.
insights.locator: The purpose of passkeys is to eliminate a shared secret

insights.claim: Labelling Pass-ta-key a novel attack surface is misleading because the same outcome — an attacker driving the credential app to log in or dump all passwords — has always been possible on any fully authenticated infected machine, and the surface extends to any data requiring authentication.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Vendor-researcher marketing inflates novelty; discount 'novel attack surface' claims from security firms when the precondition is full device compromise.
insights.quote: Pass-ta-key is a fact of life that has existed for as long as computing security has. There’s nothing novel here, and the attack surface extends to any data that requires authentication for access.
insights.locator: This risk has always been present

insights.claim: The disclosure's real value is user education: once a device — particularly a Windows one — is compromised while logged in to an account, all data stored there is available to the attacker.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Endpoint compromise remains the terminal failure mode, so security budgets should weight device integrity over credential-format upgrades.
insights.quote: once a device—particularly one running Windows—is compromised while it’s logged in to an account, all data stored there is free for the taking.
insights.locator: The purpose of passkeys is to eliminate a shared secret

insights.claim: Confusion generated by the Pass-ta-key writeup among both end users and security professionals is itself a risk to passkey adoption, since it makes people question whether the mechanism is safe at all.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Adoption of phishing-resistant auth can be slowed by messaging noise as much as by technical gaps — a headwind for identity vendors betting on fast passkey migration.
insights.quote: the research has generated confusion among end users and security professionals as they assess whether this new mechanism is truly safe to use
insights.locator: Last week, a researcher outlined what he said was a “novel attack surface”
